traits.flowering_months.note: iNaturalist research-grade records on GBIF in the south and central Puget Sound lowlands (46.7 to 48.0° N, 122.0 to 123.1° W; counted 2026-10-14): 179 records annotated as flowering (Mar 1, Apr 148, May 29, Jun 1); stated as the months holding at least a tenth of them, April and May. FEIS (Sambucus racemosa) gives April to July for Washington.

traits.fruiting_months.note: USA National Phenology Network observations (Nature's Notebook) at lowland sites west of the Cascades in Washington and Oregon (below 300 m, west of 121.8° W; 2009 to 2026, fetched 2026-10-14): 24 plant-years at 10 sites seen with ripe fruit, by the months they were seen in (May 4, Jun 12, Jul 14, Aug 2, Oct 1, Nov 1); stated as the months with at least a third as many as the busiest, June and July. FEIS (Sambucus racemosa): ripe from June to August in western Oregon.

traits.height_max_m.note: Abrams and Ferris vol. 4 (1960), as Sambucus pubens: grows 2 m to 5 m tall.

generator.params.path_half.note: A choice of the model's (crown form step B, broadleaf revision 11): the wood from the base at which a shoot's nodes are half as long, fitted so the plant grows to the height of its oldest reference size, with the crown's width left to grow inside the loose region.

generator.params.note: Hand-set from general knowledge of the species: a tall, coarse shrub with opposite pinnate leaves of sharp-toothed leaflets and dome-shaped clusters of bright red berries. Not fitted to measurements.

allometry.note: Rough sizes from general knowledge of the species: 3.5 m tall at 12 years in the open. Replace with measured data before calling this species calibrated.

appearance.note: Colours chosen by eye: mid-green leaflets; red berry clusters; grey-brown warty bark. Fruit (plant roadmap P4), as in mid-July: dome-shaped clusters of bright red berries about 5 mm across. Its year (appearance.organs.bloom.season) takes its days of bud, flower, fruit, ripe and fall from the months it flowers and fruits in, by the rules at the flowering plants (development, 2026-10-14); until then they were authored from general knowledge of the species in the south Puget Sound lowlands: creamy pyramidal clusters in April and May; berries red in late June and July, eaten by August. The forest's packages show day 196 (mid-July) until the phenology of plant roadmap P5 sets the day from the date and the local climate. Bark pattern (plant roadmap P4, `bark_pattern`): grey-brown bark with conspicuous warty lenticels; set from general knowledge of the species, not measured.

taxon.note: Scientific and common names (and USDA symbol, where given) as the spec's authors wrote them, and the genus the scientific name is written in.

growth_form.note: The growth form the spec's authors chose from the plant's habit.

growth.note: The growth plan (years, step, keyframes) chosen for growing and rendering, not a botanical fact.

variants.note: The environments, conditions and seeds chosen for growing and rendering, not a botanical fact.

taxon.family.note: WCVP v16's family for the accepted name.

taxon.plant_name_id.note: WCVP v16's plant_name_id for the accepted species the name resolves to (the accepted name).

appearance.organs.bloom.season.flower_lo.note: Its flowers drawn one by one (spec rework L1b): cream flowers 3 to 6 mm across with five recurved lobes, from pink buds. From general descriptions of the species (OregonFlora, the Flora of North America and nursery and extension pages as quoted in search results; the pages themselves were not read). The size is the flower's width, or a closed corolla's length, over the fruit's length, roughly as in life. Its flower laid out whorl by whorl (spec rework P5b): five creamy petals spread flat between five small sepals on the inferior ovary, five stamens and a pistil of four carpels, from the characters of Viburnaceae by the rules at the flowering plants.

appearance.organs.bloom.season.bud_look.note: Pink buds, a third of the flower's width, as described for the species.

traits.inflorescence.note: Jepson eFlora's account of the species, as quoted in search results (the page itself was not read): inflorescence a terminal panicle of cymes, generally more or less dome-shaped, 4 to 12 cm across, its central axis generally dominant. Its cluster is drawn as a panicle of nine cymes, its lower branches longest, so it stands broad and dome-shaped (Abrams vol. 4: "commonly broadly ovoid and dense").

traits.fruit_type.note: Idžojtić, Dendrology (2019) p. 613, Sambucus racemosa: fruit type drupe.
